name: closure-of-operations
intent: Define a value type's operations so that their arguments and their results are that same type, so that combinations compose freely and the type's interface depends on no other concept.
problem: Callers that combine two model values fall back to primitives: an addition returns a raw amount, an interval intersection returns two dates, an append returns a bare collection - and every call site has to know how to rebuild a valid instance. Combination rules scatter across call sites, results are not guaranteed to satisfy the type's invariant, and the type's public interface leaks foreign concepts.
context: Rich value types - money, quantities, ranges, paths, sets with domain semantics - where the type is immutable, has a canonical representation and every result must satisfy its invariant. Most valuable when the type's operations have an arithmetic or algebraic flavour (sum, union, intersection, append, extend) and when callers chain or accumulate results; entities qualify only for the rare operations that genuinely yield another entity.
benefits: Composability: because arguments and result are the same type, a + b + c, folds and reductions over a collection of the type stay inside the type's own vocabulary without adapters.

The interface depends on nothing else: a closed operation names no foreign type, so callers cannot couple to the representation or to raw primitives (Evans: "a high-level interface without introducing any dependency on other concepts").
Invariants survive every combination: each operation re-establishes the type's invariant once, inside the type, instead of asking every call site to rebuild a valid instance.
Callers read the domain's own vocabulary: sum, union, intersect and append read like the language domain experts use, and the arithmetic metaphor makes the outcome predictable.
Reuse by composition rather than configuration: generic algorithms (reduce/fold, iterator pipelines, monoid-style accumulation) apply to the type without special cases.
Testability: same-type inputs and outputs make property-based checks (associativity, commutativity, identity, idempotence) cheap and fixtures trivial.

Algebraic reasoning: closed operations begin to exhibit the laws of abstract algebra (associativity, identity, commutativity), enabling mathematicians and programmers alike to reason about combinations predictably, as Evans observed: the design starts to "look like arithmetic" (Seemann, 2017).
tradeoffs: Not every useful operation can be closed: comparisons, projections, conversions, scalar scaling and operations that can fail inherently return another type or no type at all, so the designer must judge each operation and accept a deliberate mix of closed and half-closed methods.

Closure is silent about laws: a closed operation need not be associative, commutative or possess an identity element (Evans' colour-mixing example is closed but only a magma), so callers and generic folds can read more algebra into the type than it actually supports.

Every closed operation must re-validate and normalise (unit, currency, scale, bounds), which concentrates failure handling inside the type: the same code becomes both the single source of truth and the single point of failure.
Value semantics are mandatory: on a mutable type the same signature mutates the receiver instead of producing a new value, and the pattern's guarantee quietly becomes an aliasing bug.
Identity elements invite invention: to make accumulation type-check, teams manufacture Money.ZERO or Employee.NOBODY and then leak those fictions into business rules.
With operator syntax the cost turns invisible - each operation allocates a new value, operators are hard to find by name search, and an overload can hide rounding, conversion or precision changes.

The abstraction can be over-applied: forcing every operation into the same-type signature when the domain has no natural combination (e.g., Money * Money, Person + Person) produces meaningless methods that corrupt the ubiquitous language.

participants.responsibility: Owns its representation and the operations on it; holds the invariant, and produces a new instance of itself for every operation that combines instances.

A named operation whose arguments and result are all the type itself (unary, binary or n-ary), named in the domain's language - add, subtract, union, intersect, append, extend - and implemented on the canonical representation.

The neutral instance an accumulation starts from and folds use as the empty case (Money.zero(currency), Interval.empty, Route.none) - defined only where the domain genuinely has one, and named in domain terms.
Code that chains or folds closed operations (a + b + c, reduce) without converting to primitives, extracting fields or rebuilding values.

use_cases: Money and quantity arithmetic in billing, pricing and accounting: Money + Money -> Money, with currency compatibility checked inside the operation.
Interval and period algebra in scheduling and effectivity modelling: intersect, union or hull of two ranges returns another range.
Geometry, physics and simulation values: vectors, matrices, complex numbers and colours whose combination law is genuinely part of the domain.
Logistics and navigation models: appending a leg to a route, extending a path, concatenating schedules - each returns the same concept.
Domain collections with set semantics: union and intersection of permission sets, tagging sets or mailing lists, keeping the collection's invariants (a Typed Collection).
Accumulation engines: folding a collection of values into a total with reduce/fold, where the closed operation plus an identity make the fold total.

Configuration and settings composition: merging configuration maps where each key's value has its own monoid (OR for booleans, MIN for timeouts, concatenation for strings), enabling layered defaults with precedence (Arolla PDF, 2018).
Event sourcing with monoidal aggregation: folding a stream of domain events into a single state object where the event type is a closed monoid over the state (Chassaing, referenced in Arolla PDF).

Supply chain impact aggregation: composing impact metrics (energy, carbon, supplier count) across a tree of suppliers where each metric forms its own closed operation, enabling parallel reduction (Arolla PDF, 2018).
Price plan and invoice composition: composing cash-flow sequences (monthly fees, annual fees, one-off options) as a monoid, eliminating combinatorial explosion of fee variants.

Interval algebra in production date-time libraries: Joda-Time's Interval.overlap(ReadableInterval) returns an Interval and NodaTime's DateInterval.Union and Intersection return a DateInterval - the same-type result re-establishes the start <= end invariant, and null (not a fabricated interval) signals an impossible combination.

Reduction APIs that codify closure as a contract: Java's Stream.reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T>) requires an accumulator whose arguments and result are all the element type, and its javadoc enforces associativity and a true identity - exactly the monoid recipe this pattern prescribes for domain values.

Set algebra in the Rust standard library: HashSet::union takes two sets and yields elements of the same element type, collected back into a HashSet - combination stays in the collection's own vocabulary without exposing its internals.
avoid_when: The operation legitimately produces another concept: comparisons (an ordering), queries (counts, projections), conversions (a primitive or a different value type). Leave these half-closed on purpose - Evans accepts this when the extra type is a primitive or a basic library class.
The type is an Entity with identity and a lifecycle: combining two instances would fabricate a lifecycle, so put the operation in a Domain Service or on the aggregate root instead.
No meaningful combination exists and closure would have to be invented (Money * Money, Person + Person): keep plain methods, or model the real relation with a different pattern.

The operation is partial or can fail (subtracting more than is available, intersecting disjoint periods): prefer an explicit result/optional type, a guard, or a Specification rather than a magic same-type value.
The decision spans several objects or requires coordinating state (cross-aggregate invariants): that is a Domain Service or an Application Service, not a type-local operation.
The type is a throwaway structural record inside one function; closure only pays off where the type has a reusable invariant.
The domain concept maps to a semigroup (associative, no identity) rather than a monoid: forcing an identity element where none exists corrupts the model. Use semigroup folds instead.
anti_patterns: Closure theatre: forcing every operation into the same-type signature — Money.times(Money), Order.combine(Order) — producing operations whose meaning nobody can state in the domain's language.
Mutating receivers behind a closed signature: add() that changes and returns the receiver, so chaining and aliasing silently corrupt shared values (the opposite of the value-object reading).
Fabricated neutral elements: Money.ZERO or Employee.NOBODY created only so loops and folds compile, then leaking into business rules as if they were real.
Presenting a half-closed interface as closed: Money.plus(Money) -> double, Range.intersect(Range) -> a pair of dates, so every caller rebuilds the type and the invariant is unenforced.
Closed operations on entities: Customer.merge(Customer) returning a customer that never existed, or Order + Order collapsing distinct lifecycles into one instance.
Overloading arithmetic operators for operations that are not arithmetic (ordering, formatting, implicit unit conversion), which makes the call site read as mathematics while doing something else.

Leaking internal representation: a closed operation that returns a primitive (double, string, tuple) because the author thought the caller 'just needs the value', breaking the type's encapsulation and forcing validation to scatter.
Forgetting associativity: a non-associative operation exposed as a foldable reduce, so a + b + c != (a + b) + c in floating-point arithmetic or in domain cases like date range concatenation.
design_principles: Value semantics and immutability: closed operations return new values and never mutate their operands.
Information hiding and no primitive obsession: the type's interface mentions only itself; the representation stays private and callers cannot pull fields out.
Cohesion and intention-revealing interfaces: the combination rules live with the data they combine and are named in the ubiquitous language.
Composition as the primary reuse mechanism: closed operations let generic algorithms (fold, reduce, pipelines) apply to the type unchanged.
Least surprise: a closed operation should obey the algebraic laws its name claims (associativity, identity, commutativity) — if it cannot, do not borrow the arithmetic metaphor.

Algebraic honesty: name and classify the operation according to its actual algebraic structure (magma, semigroup, monoid) so that callers and refactoring tools can reason about it correctly (Seemann, 2017).
best_practices: Keep the value type immutable; build each result from the canonical representation so every closed operation re-establishes the invariant.
Name operations in the domain's language and keep the arithmetic metaphor only where it is true (add, subtract, union, intersect, append); otherwise use a plain verb.
When an operation is only half-closed — a scalar factor, a comparison, a projection — give it a distinct name and signature and document that choice instead of faking closure.
Define an identity element only if the domain has one, name it in domain terms, and keep it out of business rules that should never see an empty value.
Enforce unit, currency and range compatibility inside the operation and fail fast (exception or result type) rather than coercing or silently converting.
Test the laws you advertise with property-based tests over same-type inputs (associativity, commutativity, identity, idempotence) — closure alone proves nothing.
In languages without operator overloading, expose plain same-type methods (or a module/package of operations over the type) and let the naming carry the metaphor.
Classify the algebraic structure explicitly (monoid, semigroup, magma) and document which laws hold; this guides callers on how to use fold/reduce safely.

Pair closure of operations with the identity element pattern for accumulation use cases, but guard the identity from leaking into business rules (e.g., price totals should never show a zero-money as a valid invoice line).

When composing configuration or settings from layered sources (defaults, per-department, per-user), treat each key's value as its own monoid and the map itself as a monoid whose combine operation delegates field-wise — enabling parallel reduction and clean precedence (Arolla, 2018).

For partial operations that can fail (e.g., subtracting more money than available), prefer returning Result<Value, Error> or Option<Value> rather than raising an exception, keeping the error channel explicit in the type system.

Avoid operator overloading for domain-specific combinations that do not share the semantics of arithmetic; prefer named methods (append, merge, hull) that cannot be mistaken for a mathematical operation.
sources: Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) - Chapter 10, Supple Design: CLOSURE OF OPERATIONS (p. 190 in the final manuscript).
Mark Seemann, 'Monoids, Semigroups, and Friends', ploeh.dk, 2017 — connects Evans' closure of operations to monoids, semigroups, and magmas from abstract algebra; provides concrete examples in C#.
Mark Seemann, 'Composite as Universal Abstraction', ploeh.dk, 2018 — shows that the Composite pattern is a monoid and that endomorphisms (functions A -> A) are always closed.
Arolla, 'Domain Modeling with Monoids', 2018 PDF — monoid patterns in domain modeling including configuration composition, supply chain impact aggregation, and price plan combination.
Scott Wlaschin, 'Domain Modeling Made Functional' — F# functional DDD, value objects as first-class domain building blocks, composable domain types and error handling.
Herberto Graca, 'DDD 10 – Supple Design', herbertograca.com, 2015 — detailed commentary on Evans' Chapter 10 supple design patterns including closure of operations.

Opus Software AG, 'DDD Concepts and Patterns - Supple Design', 2019 — covers intention-revealing interfaces, side-effect-free functions, assertions, conceptual contours and closure of operations as a unified group.

DDD Chapter 10 discussion (Eric Evans, 2009) — extended conversation where Evans explains the rationale for closure of operations and its relationship to conceptual contours, side-effect-free functions and value objects.
Khalil Stemmler, 'Intention Revealing Interfaces', stemmler.com, 2019 — practical TypeScript examples of intention-revealing interfaces as part of DDD supple design.
Milan Jovanovic, 'Value Objects in .NET (DDD Fundamentals)', milanjovanovic.tech, 2023 — modern .NET implementation of value objects with records and EF Core complex types.

Joda-Time 'Interval' API documentation — immutable interval whose overlap() and gap() return Interval results (null when no such interval exists), a production case of closed interval algebra with honestly partial operations.
Noda Time 'DateInterval' API documentation — Intersection and Union return a nullable DateInterval with end >= start guaranteed, closed same-type combination for date ranges in .NET.

Java SE 'Stream' API documentation — the JDK encodes closure of operations as a contract: BinaryOperator<T> combines values of one type, and the reduce javadoc enforces associativity and identity for sequential and parallel reduction.
Rust standard library 'HashSet::Union' documentation — set union as a closed operation over two sets of a common element type.

Mark Seemann, 'Towards better abstractions' (2010) and 'Better abstractions revisited' (2019) — proposes interfaces closed over their own input types as a composability heuristic and warns that algebraic closure alone does not guarantee the abstraction is meaningful.

'Some confusion with Closure of Operations' (Stack Overflow) — practitioner discussion of the ambiguity between the narrow reading (same argument and return types) and the broad reading (receiver as implicit argument), and the caution that closure is a guideline, not a universal rule.

related_patterns_notes.value-object: Closure of operations is the natural home for value objects; every value object operation that combines two values should ideally be closed, and value-object immutability is a prerequisite for the pattern's guarantees; bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.monoid: A monoid is a closed binary operation that is associative and has an identity element — the strongest algebraic form of closure of operations (Seemann, 2017). Not all closed operations are monoids; some are only semigroups (no identity) or magmas (no laws); bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.semigroup: A semigroup is an associative closed binary operation without a required identity element. Many domain combinations are semigroups (e.g., convex hull, min/max) — use this when the domain has no natural empty case; bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.side-effect-free-function: Closed operations on immutable value objects are naturally side-effect-free; together they form the backbone of Evans' supple design, making complex calculations predictable and safe to compose (Graca, 2015); bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.intention-revealing-interface: Closed operations should be named in the ubiquitous language so that callers can predict their behaviour from their signature alone, fulfilling the intention-revealing contract (Evans, p.247; Stemmler, 2019); bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.conceptual-contour: Conceptual contours guide the decomposition of a domain into cohesive types; closure of operations is the internal coherence criterion for whether an operation belongs on a type (Evans chapter 10 discussion, 2009); bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.function-composition: Closed operations compose naturally with function composition (f ∘ g); in functional languages, closed operations on algebraic data types are the primary mechanism for building rich domain models from simple parts (Wlaschin, Domain Modeling Made Functional); bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.assertion: Assertions document and enforce the preconditions, postconditions and invariants of closed operations; a closed operation's invariant check (currency compatibility, range bounds) is an assertion that the type re-establishes on every combination; bidirectional
related_patterns_notes.specification: A Specification that combines with AND/OR returns a new Specification, exhibiting closure; partial operations that can fail should be expressed as Specifications or result types rather than same-type values.
related_patterns_notes.composite: The Composite design pattern is, under the hood, a monoid: when composed objects return values that form a monoid, those values can be reduced to a single result (Seemann, 2018).
